claim: miR-9 is an evolutionarily conserved miRNA that is abundantly expressed in Area X, a basal ganglia nucleus required for vocal learning in songbirds.
source: miR-9 is an evolutionarily conserved miRNA that is abundantly expressed in Area X, a basal ganglia nucleus required for vocal learning in songbirds.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about miR-9 conservation and its expression pattern in Area X, as well as citations to prior work.

claim: Overexpression of miR-9 in Area X of juvenile zebra finches impairs developmental vocal learning.
source: Here, we report that overexpression of miR-9 in Area X of juvenile zebra finches impairs developmental vocal learning, resulting in a song with syllable omission, reduced similarity to the tutor song, and altered acoustic features.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing behavioral deficits in miR-9 overexpressing birds.

claim: miR-9 overexpression in juveniles results in songs with syllable omission.
source: Here, we report that overexpression of miR-9 in Area X of juvenile zebra finches impairs developmental vocal learning, resulting in a song with syllable omission, reduced similarity to the tutor song, and altered acoustic features.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing syllable omission in miR-9 pupils compared to controls.

claim: miR-9 overexpression in juveniles results in reduced similarity to the tutor song.
source: Here, we report that overexpression of miR-9 in Area X of juvenile zebra finches impairs developmental vocal learning, resulting in a song with syllable omission, reduced similarity to the tutor song, and altered acoustic features.
evidence: This claim is supported by motif similarity score data comparing miR-9 and control pupils.

claim: miR-9 overexpression in juveniles leads to more variable song performance in adulthood.
source: miR-9 overexpression in juveniles also leads to more variable song performance in adulthood, and abolishes social context-dependent modulation of song variability.
evidence: This claim is supported by data on syllable transition entropy and acoustic feature variability in adult birds.

claim: miR-9 overexpression abolishes social context-dependent modulation of song variability.
source: miR-9 overexpression in juveniles also leads to more variable song performance in adulthood, and abolishes social context-dependent modulation of song variability.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that miR-9 pupils fail to reduce variability in directed songs compared to undirected songs.

claim: Behavioral deficits from miR-9 overexpression are accompanied by downregulation of FoxP1 and FoxP2.
source: We further show that these behavioral deficits are accompanied by downregulation of FoxP1 and FoxP2, genes that are known to be associated with language impairments, as well as by disruption of dopamine signaling and widespread changes in the expression of genes that are important in circuit development and functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR and Western blot data showing reduced FoxP1 and FoxP2 expression.

claim: FoxP1 and FoxP2 are genes known to be associated with language impairments.
source: We further show that these behavioral deficits are accompanied by downregulation of FoxP1 and FoxP2, genes that are known to be associated with language impairments, as well as by disruption of dopamine signaling and widespread changes in the expression of genes that are important in circuit development and functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on FOXP1 and FOXP2 mutations in humans.

claim: Behavioral deficits from miR-9 overexpression are accompanied by disruption of dopamine signaling.
source: We further show that these behavioral deficits are accompanied by downregulation of FoxP1 and FoxP2, genes that are known to be associated with language impairments, as well as by disruption of dopamine signaling and widespread changes in the expression of genes that are important in circuit development and functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing downregulation of D1R and DARPP-32.

claim: Behavioral deficits from miR-9 overexpression are accompanied by widespread changes in the expression of genes important in circuit development and functions.
source: We further show that these behavioral deficits are accompanied by downregulation of FoxP1 and FoxP2, genes that are known to be associated with language impairments, as well as by disruption of dopamine signaling and widespread changes in the expression of genes that are important in circuit development and functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data showing changes in expression of 26 out of 37 tested genes.

claim: Dysregulation of miR-9 in humans may contribute to language impairments and related neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: These findings demonstrate a vital role for miR-9 in basal ganglia function and vocal communication, suggesting that dysregulation of miR-9 in humans may contribute to language impairments and related neurodevelopmental disorders.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the songbird data to human language.

claim: Juvenile songbirds learn to sing by imitating the songs of an adult tutor early in life.
source: Like humans developing speech and language, juvenile songbirds learn to sing by imitating the songs of an adult tutor early in life (Doupe and Kuhl, 1999; Immelmann and Hinde, 1969; Marler and Tamura, 1964; Tchernichovski et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on songbird vocal learning.

claim: Juvenile zebra finches begin to vocalize at about post-hatching day 30.
source: Juvenile zebra finches (pupils) first hear and memorize a tutor's song, and then, at about post-hatching day 30 (30 d), the pupils begin to vocalize.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about zebra finch development.

claim: Through thousands of trial-and-error practice sessions guided by auditory feedback, the juvenile song gradually matures into a stereotyped adult song that resembles the tutor's song.
source: Through thousands of trial-and-error practice sessions guided by auditory feedback, the juvenile song gradually matures into a stereotyped adult song that resembles the tutor's song (Immelmann and Hinde, 1969; Konishi, 1965; Tchernichovski et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on vocal learning.

claim: Adult male zebra finches sing a courtship song directed toward a female (DS) or an undirected song (UDS) when singing alone.
source: Depending on the social context, adult males sing a courtship song directed toward a female (DS) or an undirected song (UDS) when singing alone (Sossinka and Bohner, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Directed songs are more stereotyped than undirected songs.
source: These two types of songs exhibit subtle differences in acoustic features, and the DS is more stereotyped than the UDS (Hessler and Doupe, 1999; Jarvis et al., 1998; Kao and Brainard, 2006; Murugan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The motor pathway controls song production.
source: The motor pathway controls song production, while the AFP, a cortical-basal ganglia circuit required for song learning and maintenance, guides motor output through a reinforcement mechanism (Bottjer et al., 1984; Brainard and Doupe, 2000; Doupe and Kuhl, 1999; Kao et al., 2005; Nottebohm et al., 1976, 1982; Olveczky et al., 2005; Simpson and Vicario, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on the song control circuit.

claim: The AFP is a cortical-basal ganglia circuit required for song learning and maintenance.
source: The motor pathway controls song production, while the AFP, a cortical-basal ganglia circuit required for song learning and maintenance, guides motor output through a reinforcement mechanism (Bottjer et al., 1984; Brainard and Doupe, 2000; Doupe and Kuhl, 1999; Kao et al., 2005; Nottebohm et al., 1976, 1982; Olveczky et al., 2005; Simpson and Vicario, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Area X is a basal ganglia nucleus within the AFP.
source: Area X is a basal ganglia nucleus within the AFP.
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge of the songbird brain.

claim: Lesions in Area X of juveniles prevent them from crystallizing their song.
source: Lesions in Area X of juveniles prevent them from crystallizing their song (Scharff and Nottebohm, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior lesion studies.

claim: Area X receives dopaminergic innervation from the midbrain ventral tegmental area (VTA).
source: Area X receives dopaminergic innervation from the midbrain ventral tegmental area (VTA), and it also modulates the activity of VTA dopaminergic neurons in response to auditory experience, implicating Area X in reinforcement learning (Ding and Perkel, 2002; Gadagkar et al., 2016; Gale and Perkel, 2006, 2010; Lewis et al., 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical and physiological studies.

claim: Area X modulates the activity of VTA dopaminergic neurons in response to auditory experience.
source: Area X receives dopaminergic innervation from the midbrain ventral tegmental area (VTA), and it also modulates the activity of VTA dopaminergic neurons in response to auditory experience, implicating Area X in reinforcement learning (Ding and Perkel, 2002; Gadagkar et al., 2016; Gale and Perkel, 2006, 2010; Lewis et al., 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: miR-9 is an evolutionarily conserved miRNA that is highly expressed in vertebrate brains.
source: miR-9 is an evolutionarily conserved miRNA that is highly expressed in vertebrate brains (Landgraf et al., 2007; Luo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the zebra finch, miR-9 is expressed in Area X.
source: In the zebra finch, miR-9 is expressed in Area X.
evidence: This claim is based on prior knowledge and data from the authors' previous work.

claim: miR-9 expression is regulated during developmental vocal learning and in adult males singing undirected songs.
source: Its expression is regulated during developmental vocal learning and in adult males singing undirected songs (Shi et al., 2013), suggesting that miR-9 plays an active role in these processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Many of the genes expressed in the nervous system have long 3'UTRs.
source: Many of the genes expressed in the nervous system have long 3'UTRs (Mayr, 2016), highlighting the importance of miRNAs in fine-tuning gene expression in nervous system development and function.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: FOXP1 and FOXP2 are a pair of paralogous transcription factors that have important roles in nervous system development.
source: FOXP1 and FOXP2 are a pair of paralogous transcription factors that have important roles in nervous system development.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about FOXP1 and FOXP2.

claim: Deletions, mutations, and copy number variations of the FOXP1 gene have been implicated in a range of neural developmental disorders, including language delay, intellectual disability, and autism spectrum disorders (ASDs).
source: Deletions, mutations, and copy number variations of the FOXP1 gene have been implicated in a range of neural developmental disorders, including language delay, intellectual disability, and autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) (Hamdan et al., 2010; Horn et al., 2010; O'Roak et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior genetic studies.

claim: Heterozygous mutations in the FOXP2 gene cause severe speech and language impairments.
source: Heterozygous mutations in the FOXP2 gene cause severe speech and language impairments (Lai et al., 2001; Vargha-Khadem et al., 1995), accompanied by structural and functional abnormalities in multiple brain regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior genetic and clinical studies.

claim: FOXP2 mutations are accompanied by structural and functional abnormalities in the basal ganglia.
source: Heterozygous mutations in the FOXP2 gene cause severe speech and language impairments (Lai et al., 2001; Vargha-Khadem et al., 1995), accompanied by structural and functional abnormalities in multiple brain regions. These regions include the basal ganglia (Watkins et al., 2002), which is thought to be a component of the distributed neural circuitry that underlies speech and language (Graham and Fisher, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior neuroimaging studies.

claim: The basal ganglia is thought to be a component of the distributed neural circuitry that underlies speech and language.
source: These regions include the basal ganglia (Watkins et al., 2002), which is thought to be a component of the distributed neural circuitry that underlies speech and language (Graham and Fisher, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: FOXP1 and FOXP2 regulate the transcription of a large number of downstream genes, many of which are critically involved in neural differentiation, neurite outgrowth, synapse formation, and synaptic transmission.
source: FOXP1 and FOXP2 regulate the transcription of a large number of downstream genes, many of which are critically involved in neural differentiation, neurite outgrowth, synapse formation, and synaptic transmission (Konopka et al., 2009; Spiteri et al., 2007; Tang et al., 2012; Vernes et al., 2007, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior genomic studies.

claim: The functional dosage of FOXP1 and FOXP2 needs to be tightly regulated.
source: Thus, the functional dosage of FOXP1 and FOXP2 needs to be tightly regulated.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the importance of FOXP1 and FOXP2 in development and the consequences of their dysregulation.

claim: miR-9 regulates the expression of FOXP2 by targeting specific sequences in its 3'UTR.
source: Recent in vitro studies have shown that miR-9 regulates the expression of FOXP2 by targeting specific sequences in its 3'UTR (Fu et al., 2014; Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior in vitro studies.

claim: miR-9 regulates avian FoxP1 in embryonic chicken spinal cord.
source: miR-9 also regulates avian FoxP1 in embryonic chicken spinal cord (Otaegi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The lentiviral vector used carries the mCherry fluorescent protein marker driven by the human ubiquitin promoter (hUBC).
source: The lentiviral vector that we used carried the mCherry fluorescent protein marker driven by the human ubiquitin promoter (hUBC) (Edbauer et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental method and is supported by citation.

claim: Lentiviruses effectively infected 293T cells in vitro.
source: When tested in vitro, these lentiviruses effectively infected 293T cells, and overexpression of miR-9 downregulated the FOXP1 and FOXP2 proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Overexpression of miR-9 downregulated the FOXP1 and FOXP2 proteins in 293T cells.
source: When tested in vitro, these lentiviruses effectively infected 293T cells, and overexpression of miR-9 downregulated the FOXP1 and FOXP2 proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In Area X injected with lenti-miR-9, miR-9 expression was increased more than three-fold compared to expression in Area X injected with lenti-control.
source: In Area X injected with lenti-miR-9, miR-9 expression was increased more than three-fold compared to expression in Area X injected with lenti-control; the expression of an unrelated miRNA, miR-124, did not change (Figure 1C and D, p < 0.0001 for miR-9 and p = 0.288 for miR-124, n = 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The expression of miR-124 did not change following lenti-miR-9 injection.
source: In Area X injected with lenti-miR-9, miR-9 expression was increased more than three-fold compared to expression in Area X injected with lenti-control; the expression of an unrelated miRNA, miR-124, did not change (Figure 1C and D, p < 0.0001 for miR-9 and p = 0.288 for miR-124, n = 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Control pupils imitated their tutors' song motif without syllable omission.
source: On the global motif structure level, control pupils imitated their tutors' song motif without syllable omission.
evidence: This claim is supported by data on syllable counting in control pupils.

claim: miR-9 pupils omitted some of their tutor's syllables and their song motifs were shorter than those of control pupils.
source: By contrast, miR-9 pupils omitted some of their tutor's syllables and their song motifs were shorter than those of control pupils (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: 5 of 6 miR-9 pupils omitted tutor syllables.
source: We found that 5 of 6 miR-9 pupils omitted tutor syllables (Figure 2C, p = 0.0075; n = 6), and that the average number of syllables per motif was reduced by 24% in miR-9 pupils compared to control pupils (Figure 2D, p = 0.0325; n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The average number of syllables per motif was reduced by 24% in miR-9 pupils compared to control pupils.
source: We found that 5 of 6 miR-9 pupils omitted tutor syllables (Figure 2C, p = 0.0075; n = 6), and that the average number of syllables per motif was reduced by 24% in miR-9 pupils compared to control pupils (Figure 2D, p = 0.0325; n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: miR-9 pupils exhibited a lower motif similarity score than control pupils.
source: We found that miR-9 pupils exhibited a lower motif similarity score than control pupils; whereas the control pupils' motif similarity score was comparable to that of untreated pupils, indicating that virus injection alone did not affect song learning (Figure 3A, p = 0.002, two-tailed Mann-Whitney U Test; n = 6 for control and miR-9 pupils; n = 4 for untreated control pupils).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Virus injection alone did not affect song learning.
source: We found that miR-9 pupils exhibited a lower motif similarity score than control pupils; whereas the control pupils' motif similarity score was comparable to that of untreated pupils, indicating that virus injection alone did not affect song learning (Figure 3A, p = 0.002, two-tailed Mann-Whitney U Test; n = 6 for control and miR-9 pupils; n = 4 for untreated control pupils).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison between control and untreated pupils.

claim: The maximum similarity score of miR-9 pupils was significantly lower than that of control pupils.
source: The maximum similarity score of miR-9 pupils was significantly lower than that of control pupils (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, p < 0.001; n = 6), suggesting that even at their best performance, miR-9 pupils were not able to produce a good copy of their tutors' song.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Even at their best performance, miR-9 pupils were not able to produce a good copy of their tutors' song.
source: The maximum similarity score of miR-9 pupils was significantly lower than that of control pupils (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, p < 0.001; n = 6), suggesting that even at their best performance, miR-9 pupils were not able to produce a good copy of their tutors' song.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the maximum similarity score data.

claim: miR-9 pupils imitated tutors' syllables less accurately than did control pupils.
source: We found that miR-9 pupils imitated tutors' syllables less accurately than did control pupils (Figure 3B and C, p = 0.002, two-tailed Mann-Whitney U Test; n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by syllable accuracy score data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The mean frequency and Wiener entropy differed between miR-9 pupils and tutors significantly more than between control pupils and tutors.
source: We found that the mean frequency and Wiener entropy differed between miR-9 pupils and tutors significantly more than between control pupils and tutors (Figure 3D, p = 0.01 for mean frequency; p = 0.006 for Wiener entropy, two-tailed Mann-Whitney U Test; n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by acoustic feature analysis data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Wiener entropy differed significantly between miR-9 pupils and their tutors, but did not differ significantly between control pupils and their tutors.
source: In addition, Wiener entropy differed significantly between miR-9 pupils and their tutors, but did not differ significantly between control pupils and their tutors (p < 0.001, t(24) = 8.245 for miR-9 pupils; p = 0.432, t(41) = 0.794 for control pupils, paired t-test; control pupils: n = 42 syllable; miR-9 pupils: n = 25 syllables; n = 6 animals per group) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The songs of miR-9 pupils often exhibited switching of syllable order, truncation of motifs, and/or syllable stuttering.
source: A careful examination of sonograms showed that the songs of miR-9 pupils often exhibited switching of syllable order, truncation of motifs, and/or syllable stuttering (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sonogram examples shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Syllable transition entropy of miR-9 pupils was significantly higher than that of control pupils.
source: We found that syllable transition entropy of miR-9 pupils was significantly higher than that of control pupils (Figure 4C, p = 0.002, two-tailed Mann-Whitney U Test; n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Duration, goodness of pitch, and Wiener entropy were significantly more variable in adult miR-9 pupils than in adult control pupils.
source: Among the acoustic features analyzed, duration, goodness of pitch, and Wiener entropy were significantly more variable in adult miR-9 pupils than in adult control pupils (Figure 4D, p = 0.009 for duration; p = 0.015 for goodness of pitch; and p = 0.009 for Wiener entropy, two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test; n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Overexpression of miR-9 in juvenile Area X leads to more variable song performance in adulthood.
source: These results indicate that overexpression of miR-9 in juvenile Area X leads to more variable song performance in adulthood.
evidence: This claim is supported by data on syllable transition entropy and acoustic feature variability.

claim: The expression of miR-9 in Area X is upregulated by singing an undirected song (UDS) but not by singing a female-directed song (DS).
source: It is known that the expression of miR-9 in Area X is upregulated by singing an undirected song (UDS) but not by singing a female-directed song (DS); furthermore, the acoustic features of UDS are more variable than those of DS (Jarvis et al., 1998; Kao and Brainard, 2006; Leblois et al., 2010; Murugan et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2013; Teramitsu and White, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The acoustic features of UDS are more variable than those of DS.
source: It is known that the expression of miR-9 in Area X is upregulated by singing an undirected song (UDS) but not by singing a female-directed song (DS); furthermore, the acoustic features of UDS are more variable than those of DS (Jarvis et al., 1998; Kao and Brainard, 2006; Leblois et al., 2010; Murugan et al., 2013; Shi et al., 2013; Teramitsu and White, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In control birds, the variability in syllable cFF was greater in UDS than in DS.
source: In control birds, the variability in syllable cFF was greater in UDS than in DS. In miR-9 pupils, however, the syllable cFF remained variable in DS, abolishing the social context-dependent modulation of syllable variability (Figure 5A and B, p = 0.006 for control pupils; p = 0.510 for miR-9 pupils, paired-t test; control pupils: n = 21 syllables, 6 animals; miR-9 pupils: n = 11 syllables, 6 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In miR-9 pupils, the syllable cFF remained variable in DS, abolishing the social context-dependent modulation of syllable variability.
source: In control birds, the variability in syllable cFF was greater in UDS than in DS. In miR-9 pupils, however, the syllable cFF remained variable in DS, abolishing the social context-dependent modulation of syllable variability (Figure 5A and B, p = 0.006 for control pupils; p = 0.510 for miR-9 pupils, paired-t test; control pupils: n = 21 syllables, 6 animals; miR-9 pupils: n = 11 syllables, 6 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Both 65 d and 80 d control pupils produced a more stereotyped DS with reduced variability in cFF.
source: Similar to the adults, the 65 d and 80 d control pupils produced a more stereotyped DS with reduced variability in cFF, whereas both 65 d and 80 d miR-9 pupils retained variability in DS (Figure 5C, p < 0.05 for 65 d and p < 0.01 for 80 d and 100 d groups, respectively; two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test; at 65 d, control pupils: n = 8 syllables, 3 animals; miR-9 pupils: n = 6 syllables, 4 animals; at 80 d, control pupils: n = 11 syllables, 5 animals; miR-9 pupils: n = 9 syllables, 5 animals; at 100 d, control pupils: n = 14 syllables, 6 animals; miR-9 pupils: n = 10 syllables, 6 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Both 65 d and 80 d miR-9 pupils retained variability in DS.
source: Similar to the adults, the 65 d and 80 d control pupils produced a more stereotyped DS with reduced variability in cFF, whereas both 65 d and 80 d miR-9 pupils retained variability in DS (Figure 5C, p < 0.05 for 65 d and p < 0.01 for 80 d and 100 d groups, respectively; two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test; at 65 d, control pupils: n = 8 syllables, 3 animals; miR-9 pupils: n = 6 syllables, 4 animals; at 80 d, control pupils: n = 11 syllables, 5 animals; miR-9 pupils: n = 9 syllables, 5 animals; at 100 d, control pupils: n = 14 syllables, 6 animals; miR-9 pupils: n = 10 syllables, 6 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: miR-9 plays a role in modulating social-context-dependent song variability.
source: Together, these results suggest that miR-9 plays a role in modulating social-context-dependent song variability.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data on cFF variability in different social contexts.

claim: At both 65 d and 80 d, miR-9 pupils imitated poorly, and their songs were less similar to the tutors' song than those of control pupils.
source: At both 65 d and 80 d, miR-9 pupils imitated poorly, and their songs were less similar to the tutors' song than those of control pupils (Figure 6A, p = 0.0022 for 65 d, 80 d and 100 d songs, two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test; n = 6 per group).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: At 150 d, the similarity score of miR-9 pupils was significantly lower than that of control pupils.
source: We found that at 150 d, the similarity score of miR-9 pupils was significantly lower than that of control pupils (Figure 6A, p = 0.008, two-tailed Mann-Whitney U Test; n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Control pupils improved the similarity score of their song as they matured.
source: While the control pupils improved the similarity score of their song as they matured, miR-9 pupils did not improve their score from 65 d to 150 d (Figure 6A, p = 0 for control pupils and p = 0.137 for miR-9 pupils, one-way ANOVA; n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: miR-9 pupils did not improve their similarity score from 65 d to 150 d.
source: While the control pupils improved the similarity score of their song as they matured, miR-9 pupils did not improve their score from 65 d to 150 d (Figure 6A, p = 0 for control pupils and p = 0.137 for miR-9 pupils, one-way ANOVA; n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: At 65 d, Wiener entropy of the control pupils and the miR-9 pupils was similar.
source: At 65 d, Wiener entropy of the control pupils and the miR-9 pupils was similar, but at both 80 d and 100 d, the Wiener entropy scores of miR-9 pupils were higher than those of the control pupils (Figure 6B, p = 0.482 for 65 d, p = 0.028 for 80 d, and p = 0.020 for 100 d, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: At both 80 d and 100 d, the Wiener entropy scores of miR-9 pupils were higher than those of the control pupils.
source: At 65 d, Wiener entropy of the control pupils and the miR-9 pupils was similar, but at both 80 d and 100 d, the Wiener entropy scores of miR-9 pupils were higher than those of the control pupils (Figure 6B, p = 0.482 for 65 d, p = 0.028 for 80 d, and p = 0.020 for 100 d, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The Wiener entropy of control pupils' syllables was reduced as they matured.
source: The Wiener entropy of control pupils' syllables was reduced as they matured, whereas the Wiener entropy of miR-9 pupils' syllables was not (Figure 6B, p = 0.002 for control pupils and p = 0.709 for miR-9 pupils, one-way ANOVA; n = 6 per group).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The Wiener entropy of miR-9 pupils' syllables was not reduced as they matured.
source: The Wiener entropy of control pupils' syllables was reduced as they matured, whereas the Wiener entropy of miR-9 pupils' syllables was not (Figure 6B, p = 0.002 for control pupils and p = 0.709 for miR-9 pupils, one-way ANOVA; n = 6 per group).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Syllable acoustic variability was reduced in songs of both control pupils and miR-9 pupils from 65 d to 100 d.
source: Syllable acoustic variability was reduced in songs of both control pupils and miR-9 pupils from 65 d to 100 d (Figure 6C–E, p < 0.001 for duration, pitch, and Wiener entropy for both control and miR-9 pupils [except p < 0.01 for duration for miR-9 pupils]; one-way ANOVA; control pupils: n = 42 syllables, 6 animals; miR-9 pupils: n = 25 syllables, 6 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: Variability in duration, pitch, and Wiener entropy was significantly higher in miR-9 pupils than in control pupils at all ages.
source: However, variability in each of these acoustic features was significantly higher in miR-9 pupils than in control pupils at all ages (Figure 6C–E, p < 0.0001 for duration, pitch, and Wiener entropy for each age, two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test; control pupils: n = 42 syllables, 6 animals; miR-9 pupils: n = 25 syllables, 6 animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: miR-9 overexpression in juvenile Area X leads to higher variability in songs throughout maturation.
source: These data indicate that miR-9 overexpression in juvenile Area X leads to higher variability in songs throughout maturation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data on acoustic feature variability during development.

claim: High level of trial-by-trial variation in acoustic features of miR-9 pupils may contribute to their inability to imitate the tutor's song accurately.
source: This high level of trial-by-trial variation in acoustic features of miR-9 pupils may contribute to their inability to imitate the tutor's song accurately.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed variability and imitation deficits.

claim: At both 65 d and 100 d, miR-9 pupils sang slightly more syllables than control pupils, but the differences were not significant.
source: We found that at both 65 d and 100 d, miR-9 pupils sang slightly more syllables than control pupils, but the differences were not significant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, p = 0.419 for 65 d; p = 0.109 for 100 d, two-tailed Mann-Whitney U Test; n = 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: It is unlikely that the amount of singing contributed to the effect of miR-9 on song learning.
source: Thus, it is unlikely that the amount of singing contributed to the effect of miR-9 on song learning.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of significant difference in singing amount between groups.

claim: The expression levels of both FoxP1 and FoxP2 mRNAs were significantly downregulated in Area X injected with lenti-miR-9 compared to Area X injected with lenti-control.
source: We found that the expression levels of both FoxP1 and FoxP2 mRNAs were significantly downregulated in Area X injected with lenti-miR-9 compared to Area X injected with lenti-control (Figure 7A, p = 0.006 for FoxP1 and p < 0.0001 for FoxP2, n = 7), whereas no change in expression of either FoxP1 or FoxP2 mRNA was found in tissue adjacent to Area X.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: No change in expression of either FoxP1 or FoxP2 mRNA was found in tissue adjacent to Area X.
source: We found that the expression levels of both FoxP1 and FoxP2 mRNAs were significantly downregulated in Area X injected with lenti-miR-9 compared to Area X injected with lenti-control (Figure 7A, p = 0.006 for FoxP1 and p < 0.0001 for FoxP2, n = 7), whereas no change in expression of either FoxP1 or FoxP2 mRNA was found in tissue adjacent to Area X.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Both FoxP1 and FoxP2 protein levels were downregulated in Area X injected with the lenti-miR-9 virus compared to controls.
source: We found that both FoxP1 and FoxP2 protein levels were also downregulated in Area X injected with the lenti-miR-9 virus compared to controls (Figure 7B, p = 0.0007 for FoxP1 and p = 0.0037 for FoxP2, n = 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Dopamine plays an important role in modulating basal ganglia circuit plasticity and song stereotypy.
source: The neurotransmitter dopamine plays an important role in modulating basal ganglia circuit plasticity and song stereotypy (Ding and Perkel, 2002; Leblois et al., 2010; Murugan et al., 2013; Sasaki et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Both the dopamine D1 (D1R) and D2 (D2R) receptors are expressed in Area X.
source: Both the dopamine D1 (D1R) and D2 (D2R) receptors are expressed in Area X (Kubikova et al., 2010), and D1R is regulated by FoxP2 (Murugan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: D1R is regulated by FoxP2.
source: Both the dopamine D1 (D1R) and D2 (D2R) receptors are expressed in Area X (Kubikova et al., 2010), and D1R is regulated by FoxP2 (Murugan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: D1R was downregulated in Area X injected with the lenti-miR-9 virus compared to Area X injected with the lenti-control virus.
source: We found that four weeks after viral injection, D1R was downregulated in Area X injected with the lenti-miR-9 virus compared to Area X injected with the lenti-control virus, whereas the expression of D2R was unchanged (Figure 7C, p < 0.0001 for D1R and p = 0.3384 for D2R, unpaired t-test; n = 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The expression of D2R was unchanged following lenti-miR-9 injection.
source: We found that four weeks after viral injection, D1R was downregulated in Area X injected with the lenti-miR-9 virus compared to Area X injected with the lenti-control virus, whereas the expression of D2R was unchanged (Figure 7C, p < 0.0001 for D1R and p = 0.3384 for D2R, unpaired t-test; n = 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: DARPP-32 is a 32 kDa dopamine- and cAMP-regulated phosphoprotein that is a major signal transduction component acting downstream of dopamine receptors.
source: DARPP-32, a 32 kDa dopamine- and cAMP-regulated phosphoprotein, is a major signal transduction component acting downstream of dopamine receptors, and is highly expressed in striatal medium spiny neurons (Greengard et al., 1999; Murugan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: DARPP-32 is highly expressed in striatal medium spiny neurons.
source: DARPP-32, a 32 kDa dopamine- and cAMP-regulated phosphoprotein, is a major signal transduction component acting downstream of dopamine receptors, and is highly expressed in striatal medium spiny neurons (Greengard et al., 1999; Murugan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: DARPP-32 protein level was significantly downregulated in Area X injected with the lenti-miR-9 virus compared to Area X injected with the lenti-control virus.
source: We found that DARPP-32 protein level was significantly downregulated in Area X injected with the lenti-miR-9 virus compared to Area X injected with the lenti-control virus (Figure 7D, p = 0.0022, unpaired t-test; n = 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: FOXP1 and FOXP2 regulate a large number of downstream transcriptional target genes that have important roles in neural circuit development and functions.
source: FOXP1 and FOXP2 regulate a large number of downstream transcriptional target genes that have important roles in neural circuit development and functions (Konopka et al., 2009; Spiteri et al., 2007; Vernes et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior genomic studies.

claim: 26 of 37 tested genes changed their expression in juvenile Area X 4 weeks after miR-9 viral injection.
source: We found widespread changes in gene expression: 26 of 37 tested genes changed their expression in juvenile Area X 4 weeks after miR-9 viral injection.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data on downstream gene expression.

claim: 15 downstream genes were upregulated and 11 were downregulated following miR-9 overexpression.
source: Consistent with the fact that FOXP1 and FOXP2 are capable of bi-directional regulation of gene expression, either enhancing or repressing gene expression (Li et al., 2004), we observed bi-directional changes in the expression of these downstream genes: 15 upregulated and 11 downregulated.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8.

claim: A majority of the changed genes increased or decreased their expression by less than 50%.
source: The magnitudes of the changes, however, were moderate; a majority of these genes increased or decreased their expression by less than 50%.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Birds with miR-9 overexpression in Area X exhibited higher trial-by-trial variability, which was reflected in a more variable sequence of syllable order, truncated motifs, and syllable stuttering.
source: Songs of birds with miR-9 overexpression in Area X exhibited higher trial-by-trial variability, which was reflected in a more variable sequence of syllable order, truncated motifs, and syllable stuttering.
evidence: This claim is supported by data on syllable transition entropy and sonogram analysis.

claim: Syntax change has not been reported in prior studies in which FoxP2 was either knocked down or overexpressed in Area X.
source: Syntax change has not been reported in prior studies in which FoxP2 was either knocked down or overexpressed in Area X (Haesler et al., 2007; Heston and White, 2015; Murugan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: That miR-9 regulates the expression of both FoxP1 and FoxP2 and potentially of other genes in Area X may explain the robust deficits in vocal learning observed.
source: That miR-9 regulates the expression of both FoxP1 and FoxP2 and potentially of other genes in Area X may explain the robust deficits in vocal learning we observed here.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed molecular and behavioral effects.

claim: Birds with miR-9 overexpression failed to modulate song variability when singing a directed song, similar to birds with reduced FoxP2 expression in adult Area X.
source: Similar to birds with reduced FoxP2 expression in adult Area X (Murugan et al., 2013), birds with miR-9 overexpression failed to modulate song variability when singing a directed song.
evidence: This claim is supported by data on cFF variability and citation to prior work.

claim: Higher miR-9 levels in Area X render the circuit permissive to a more variable song or interfere with the production of a more stereotyped directed song.
source: It appears that, whether naturally or artificially induced, higher miR-9 levels in Area X render the circuit permissive to a more variable song or interfere with the production of a more stereotyped directed song.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed effects of miR-9 on song variability.

claim: The effects of miR-9 overexpression on song imitation were apparent at 65 days after hatching, and these birds failed to improve their imitation thereafter.
source: The effects of miR-9 overexpression on song imitation were apparent at 65 days after hatching, and these birds failed to improve their imitation thereafter (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The developmental vocal learning process is accompanied with a gradual increase in the miR-9 level in Area X, reaching its high point as juveniles become adults.
source: In normal birds, the developmental vocal learning process is accompanied with a gradual increase in the miR-9 level in Area X, reaching its high point as juveniles become adults, and songs become stabilized; meanwhile, throughout the process, the FoxP2 level gradually decreases (Haesler et al., 2004; Shi et al., 2013; Teramitsu et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Throughout the developmental vocal learning process, the FoxP2 level gradually decreases.
source: In normal birds, the developmental vocal learning process is accompanied with a gradual increase in the miR-9 level in Area X, reaching its high point as juveniles become adults, and songs become stabilized; meanwhile, throughout the process, the FoxP2 level gradually decreases (Haesler et al., 2004; Shi et al., 2013; Teramitsu et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: An artificially increased miR-9 level does not result in premature stabilization of a juvenile's song nor in an increase in similarity to the tutor's song.
source: Our current data indicate that an artificially increased miR-9 level (and reduced FoxP2 level) does not result in premature stabilization of a juvenile's song nor in an increase in similarity to the tutor's song.
evidence: This claim is supported by data on song development in miR-9 overexpressing birds.

claim: miR-9 overexpression appears to lock Area X in a plasticity-dominant state, preventing further progression toward song stereotypy.
source: Rather, miR-9 overexpression appears to lock Area X in a plasticity-dominant state, preventing further progression toward song stereotypy.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed effects on song variability and development.

claim: Lesions in lMAN lead to a prematurely stabilized song.
source: While lesions in lMAN lead to a prematurely stabilized song, birds with Area X lesions never achieve song stability as control birds do (Scharff and Nottebohm, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior lesion studies.

claim: Birds with Area X lesions never achieve song stability as control birds do.
source: While lesions in lMAN lead to a prematurely stabilized song, birds with Area X lesions never achieve song stability as control birds do (Scharff and Nottebohm, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior lesion studies.

claim: The effect of miR-9 overexpression might be restrained by circuit functions, in this case functions of Area X.
source: Although the experimental approaches used in these studies are unrelated (molecular manipulation vs. electrolytic lesion), our observations are more aligned with the effects of lesions in Area X, suggesting that the effect of miR-9 overexpression (gene manipulation) might be restrained by circuit functions, in this case functions of Area X.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from comparison with lesion studies.

claim: Area X and the AFP guide song motor learning through processes that evaluate the motor output patterns according to auditory feedback, and reinforce favorable motor actions.
source: According to the reinforcement learning theory, Area X and the AFP guide song motor learning through processes that evaluate the motor output patterns according to auditory feedback, and reinforce favorable motor actions.
evidence: This claim is based on established reinforcement learning theory applied to songbird vocal learning.

claim: Dopamine levels in Area X are higher when birds sing DS.
source: Dopamine levels in Area X are higher when birds sing DS (Sasaki et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Blocking D1R pharmacologically or reducing D1R expression by knocking down FoxP2 in Area X results in a more variable DS.
source: Blocking D1R pharmacologically or reducing D1R expression by knocking down FoxP2 in Area X results in a more variable DS (Leblois et al., 2010; Murugan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The downregulation of D1R but not D2R in Area X may have produced a functional imbalance between the two signaling pathways, which may have contributed to impaired song learning and performance.
source: The downregulation of D1R but not D2R in Area X, as a consequence of miR-9 overexpression, may have produced a functional imbalance between the two signaling pathways, which may have contributed to impaired song learning and performance.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed molecular changes and behavioral deficits.

claim: The D1R-expressing direct pathway and the D2R-expressing indirect pathway act in an opposing but coordinated manner in the basal ganglia to finely control the timing and synchronization of motor actions.
source: Studies in mammals suggest that the D1R-expressing direct pathway and the D2R-expressing indirect pathway act in an opposing but coordinated manner in the basal ganglia to finely control the timing and synchronization of motor actions; imbalances between the two pathways may lead to movement and cognitive disorders (Cazorla et al., 2015; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on mammalian basal ganglia.

claim: Imbalances between the D1R and D2R pathways may lead to movement and cognitive disorders.
source: Studies in mammals suggest that the D1R-expressing direct pathway and the D2R-expressing indirect pathway act in an opposing but coordinated manner in the basal ganglia to finely control the timing and synchronization of motor actions; imbalances between the two pathways may lead to movement and cognitive disorders (Cazorla et al., 2015; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The miR-9–FoxP2–dopamine signaling network provides a mechanism that dynamically adjusts the functional balance between the D1R and D2R signaling pathways.
source: Thus, the miR-9–FoxP2–dopamine signaling network provides a mechanism that dynamically adjusts the functional balance between the D1R and D2R signaling pathways, allowing birds to adapt to the changing maturation state of song in juveniles and to modulate song stereotypy according to the social context in which a song is produced.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed molecular and behavioral effects.

claim: Many of the FOXP1 and FOXP2 downstream transcriptional target genes were identified by genome-wide chromatin immunoprecipitation assays.
source: Many of the FOXP1 and FOXP2 downstream transcriptional target genes were identified by genome-wide chromatin immunoprecipitation assays, which depend on the binding of transcription factors FOXP1 or FOXP2 to promoter sequences (Konopka et al., 2009; Spiteri et al., 2007; Vernes et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior genomic studies.

claim: The changes in expression of downstream genes in Area X when FoxP1 and FoxP2 were downregulated by miR-9 provides further evidence for a regulatory relationship between these genes and FOXP1 or FOXP2 in the basal ganglia circuit critical for vocal communication.
source: The changes in expression of these downstream genes in Area X when FoxP1 and FoxP2 were downregulated by miR-9 provides further evidence for a regulatory relationship between these genes and FOXP1 or FOXP2 in the basal ganglia circuit critical for vocal communication.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed gene expression changes.

claim: CNTNAP2 and DISC1 have each been implicated in multiple disorders, including language impairments, ASDs, ADHD, intellectual disabilities, and schizophrenia.
source: Among the genes we tested, CNTNAP2 and DISC1 have each been implicated in multiple disorders, including language impairments, ASDs, ADHD, intellectual disabilities, and schizophrenia (Fromer et al., 2016; Purcell et al., 2014), suggesting that these neural developmental disorders, cognitive impairments, and psychiatric disorders share common molecular substrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neural developmental disorders, cognitive impairments, and psychiatric disorders share common molecular substrates.
source: Among the genes we tested, CNTNAP2 and DISC1 have each been implicated in multiple disorders, including language impairments, ASDs, ADHD, intellectual disabilities, and schizophrenia (Fromer et al., 2016; Purcell et al., 2014), suggesting that these neural developmental disorders, cognitive impairments, and psychiatric disorders share common molecular substrates.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the overlap in genes implicated in multiple disorders.

claim: Distinct but overlapping phenotypes are manifested depending on where and when genes are expressed and how they are regulated.
source: It is possible that distinct but overlapping phenotypes are manifested depending on where and when these genes are expressed and how they are regulated, emphasizing the need to study these genes in the context of specific functional neural circuits.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed gene expression patterns and behavioral effects.

claim: miR-9 is expressed in the embryonic human brain.
source: miR-9 is expressed in the embryonic human brain and has been shown to regulate human FOXP2 gene expression (Fu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: miR-9 has been shown to regulate human FOXP2 gene expression.
source: miR-9 is expressed in the embryonic human brain and has been shown to regulate human FOXP2 gene expression (Fu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: It is likely that miR-9 plays a role in human language development by fine-tuning FOXP1 and FOXP2 expression.
source: It is likely that miR-9 plays a role in human language development by fine-tuning FOXP1 and FOXP2 expression, thereby coordinating the expression of a large number of genes that are active in neural development and function.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the songbird data to human language.

claim: Both FOXP1 and FOXP2 mRNAs have long 3'UTRs containing numerous miRNA binding sites.
source: Both FOXP1 and FOXP2 mRNAs have long 3'UTRs containing numerous miRNA binding sites, suggesting that these genes can be regulated by many miRNAs in addition to miR-9.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of mRNA structure and miRNA regulation.

claim: FOXP1 and FOXP2 can be regulated by many miRNAs in addition to miR-9.
source: Both FOXP1 and FOXP2 mRNAs have long 3'UTRs containing numerous miRNA binding sites, suggesting that these genes can be regulated by many miRNAs in addition to miR-9.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the presence of multiple miRNA binding sites in the 3'UTRs.

claim: Dysregulation of miRNAs or of miRNA–FOXP1/FOXP2 interactions by genetic, environmental, or physiological factors may contribute to language impairments and related neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: Dysregulation of these miRNAs or of miRNA–FOXP1/FOXP2 interactions by genetic, environmental, or physiological factors, thus, may contribute to language impairments and related neurodevelopmental disorders.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed effects of miR-9 dysregulation.

claim: There was no difference in total Area X volume between the non-injected and injected groups.
source: There was no difference in total Area X volume between the non-injected and injected groups, and there was no difference in total Area X volume between the lenti-control- and lenti-miR-9-injected groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There was no difference in total Area X volume between the lenti-control- and lenti-miR-9-injected groups.
source: There was no difference in total Area X volume between the non-injected and injected groups, and there was no difference in total Area X volume between the lenti-control- and lenti-miR-9-injected groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Similar numbers of Hu+ neurons were found in Area X of non-injected animals and in Area X injected with the lenti-control virus or with the lenti-miR-9 virus.
source: We found similar numbers of Hu+ neurons in Area X of non-injected animals and in Area X injected with the lenti-control virus or with the lenti-miR-9 virus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Physical damage to Area X caused by viral injection, if any, was minimal.
source: These results indicate that physical damage to Area X caused by viral injection, if any, was minimal; thus, the behavioral phenotypes that we observed are likely due to virally transduced miR-9 overexpression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of differences in Area X volume and neuron number.

claim: The behavioral phenotypes observed are likely due to virally transduced miR-9 overexpression.
source: These results indicate that physical damage to Area X caused by viral injection, if any, was minimal; thus, the behavioral phenotypes that we observed are likely due to virally transduced miR-9 overexpression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of physical damage and the specificity of miR-9 overexpression.
